title: Fate, providence, or chaos
hookLine: either fate, or providence, or confusion; in each case keep your own mind (Meditations 12.14)

cards: You're waiting for news you can't control. The test result. The job decision.
The storm track on the weather map. Underneath the waiting sits a bigger question nobody can settle for you: is any of this planned? Is someone watching over it?
Or is it all just weather? In this entry, at least, Marcus doesn't claim to settle it. He writes down all three answers.

teach.b: First, three possibilities. Either there's a fixed necessity, an order that can't be broken, Marcus writes; or a providence that can be moved by prayer; or a confusion with no purpose and no one directing it.
Second, an answer for each. If it's unbreakable necessity, why resist it? If it's a providence that listens, make yourself worthy of help from the divine.

teach.h: THE STORM CAN'T TAKE THE MIND.
teach.b: If it's chaos with no one in charge, be content that in such a storm you have within you a mind that can steer. Third, the storm.
And if the storm carries you off, he says, let it carry off the flesh, the breath, everything else. It won't carry off the mind. Fourth, why three.
Some readers hear in the three the rival answers of his own day: a world of fixed order, a providence that listens, a world of chance. Marcus doesn't settle that argument here, and he ranks no one.
He does something more practical: he makes sure his answer works whichever is true.
In each case the work is the same: keep your own mind steady. You don't have to decide the biggest question before you can steady yourself inside it.

how: Readers of Marcus sometimes use this three-way reflection during uncertain waits, choosing a response that holds whether events are fated, guided or random.

o: a fixed order that can't be broken, one of three options
the one answer Marcus was sure ran the world
a goddess Romans prayed to for luck in battle

games.q: fate, providence, or chaos — tap the pairs.
p: you still have a mind that steers

s: Marcus settles which of the three is true
he gives an answer that works under each, and leaves the big question open.
he says even a storm that carries off the body can't carry off the mind
let it take the flesh and the breath, he writes; not the mind.

games.q: you're waiting for news you can't control, and you don't know whether anything is guiding it. you're Marcus. what do you do?
o: decide first whether the universe is ordered.
whichever it is, keep your own mind steady.
games.why: fate, providence, or chaos, he writes: each has a fitting response, and in each the mind stays your own.

practice: Bring to mind one uncertainty you're living with, and let it stay uncertain.

Try each of Marcus's answers on it: if it's settled already, I can stop fighting it; if someone is listening, I can try to be worthy of help; if it's all chance, I still have my own mind. Notice which one steadies you.

wordCard.voice: Fate. Marcus's three possibilities: fate, providence, or chaos. Whichever is true, keep your own mind steady. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: providence, forethought. one of Marcus's three possibilities.

carryVoice: Your line: keep my mind. The storm can take a lot, but not that. Day six hundred thirty-one, done.
